title: CUET Physics Test 15
subject: Physics (Code: 322)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Physics - 322.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Physics papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format and level (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Physics, Class XII, Parts I and II (rationalised edition)
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
Calculators are not allowed; numbers are chosen so the working can be done by hand.

questions.sub_topic: Current when 30 C passes in one minute
questions.question: A charge of 30 C flows through a wire in 1 minute. The current is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.5 A
Given: \(Q = 30\) C, \(t = 60\) s
Formula: \(I = \dfrac{Q}{t}\)
Step 1: \(I = \dfrac{30}{60} = 0.5\) A
Common mistake: 30 A (A) forgets to convert minutes to seconds.
Key point: Current is charge per second.

questions.sub_topic: Observations and what they reveal about atoms and nuclei
questions.question:
Match each observation in List-I with the conclusion it supports in List-II.

List-I
(A) Most α-particles pass through gold foil undeflected
(B) A few α-particles bounce back
(C) Hydrogen emits only certain wavelengths
(D) Binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant for \(30 < A < 170\)

List-II
(I) Positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
(II) The nuclear force is short-ranged
(III) Atomic energy levels are quantised
(IV) Most of the atom is empty space
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Free passage means little in the way (IV)
Step 2: Reversal needs a heavy, concentrated positive charge (I)
Step 3: Fixed wavelengths mean fixed energy jumps (III)
Step 4: Each nucleon binds only to its near neighbours (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); the rare back-scattering is what reveals the nucleus.
Key point: Each key observation forced a new idea about atoms and nuclei.

questions.sub_topic: Output frequency of a half-wave rectifier on 50 Hz
questions.question: A half-wave rectifier is fed from a 50 Hz supply. The frequency of its output pulses is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 50 Hz
Given: \(\nu = 50\) Hz
Formula: half-wave rectification passes one half of each cycle
Step 1: One pulse per cycle: 50 Hz
Common mistake: 100 Hz (B) is the full-wave value.
Key point: Half-wave output repeats once per input cycle.

questions.sub_topic: Load and power for maximum transfer from a 12 V battery
questions.question: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance \(2\ \Omega\) is connected to a variable load. The load resistance that receives the most power, and that power, are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2\ \Omega\) and 18 W
Given: \(\varepsilon = 12\) V, \(r = 2\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(P = \dfrac{\varepsilon^2R}{(R + r)^2}\), which is greatest when \(R = r\)
Step 1: \(R = 2\ \Omega\), so \(I = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3\) A
Step 2: \(P = I^2R = 9 \times 2 = 18\) W
Common mistake: (C) gives the total power at short circuit, all of it wasted inside the battery. (D) gives 16 W at \(4\ \Omega\), which is less than 18 W.
Key point: A load matched to the internal resistance gets the most power.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Kinetic energy of a neutron of wavelength 0.1 nm
questions.question: A neutron (\(m = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\) kg) has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.1 nm. Its kinetic energy is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.082 eV
Given: \(\lambda = 10^{-10}\) m, \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s
Formula: \(K = \dfrac{h^2}{2m\lambda^2}\)
Step 1: \(K = \dfrac{4.4 \times 10^{-67}}{2 \times 1.675 \times 10^{-27} \times 10^{-20}} \approx 1.31 \times 10^{-20}\) J
Step 2: \(K \approx 0.082\) eV
Common mistake: 150 eV (A) is the value for an electron. 12.4 keV (B) is for a photon of that wavelength.
Key point: For the same wavelength, a heavier particle needs far less energy.

questions.sub_topic: Four radiations in increasing order of frequency
questions.question:
Arrange these radiations in increasing order of frequency:
(A) the 21 cm radio line of hydrogen
(B) X-rays of wavelength 1 nm
(C) infrared of wavelength 10 μm
(D) ultraviolet of wavelength 300 nm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C), (D), (B)
Step 1: \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\): (A) \(1.4 \times 10^9\) Hz; (C) \(3 \times 10^{13}\) Hz
Step 2: (D) \(1 \times 10^{15}\) Hz; (B) \(3 \times 10^{17}\) Hz
Step 3: Increasing: (A), (C), (D), (B)
Common mistake: (B) is in decreasing order of frequency, which is increasing order of wavelength.
Key point: The longer the wavelength, the lower the frequency.

questions.sub_topic: Huygens' principle and wavefronts — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A point source in a uniform medium gives spherical wavefronts.
(B) Huygens' secondary wavelets also produce a wave travelling back towards the source.
(C) In an isotropic medium, rays are perpendicular to the wavefronts.
(D) Far from a source, a small part of a spherical wavefront is nearly plane.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: Huygens' construction takes only the forward envelope of the wavelets; there is no backwave.
Why not the others: (A) the wave spreads equally in all directions. (C) rays show the direction of travel. (D) the radius is very large. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The new wavefront is the forward envelope of the secondary wavelets.

questions.sub_topic: Angular size of the Moon's image in a telescope
questions.question: A telescope in normal adjustment has \(f_o = 150\) cm and \(f_e = 5\) cm. The Moon subtends \(0.5^\circ\) at the objective. The angle its final image subtends at the eye is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(15^\circ\)
Given: \(f_o = 150\) cm, \(f_e = 5\) cm, \(\alpha = 0.5^\circ\)
Formula: \(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\)
Step 1: \(m = 30\)
Step 2: \(\beta = 30 \times 0.5^\circ = 15^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(15.5^\circ\) (C) uses the tube length, \(\dfrac{155}{5}\). \(0.017^\circ\) (A) divides by the magnification.
Key point: A telescope magnifies angles, not sizes.

questions.sub_topic: Potential energy of +1 μC and +4 μC 20 cm apart
questions.question: The electric potential energy of charges \(+1\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(+4\ \mu\text{C}\) placed 20 cm apart is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.18 J
Given: \(q_1 = 10^{-6}\) C, \(q_2 = 4 \times 10^{-6}\) C, \(r = 0.2\) m
Formula: \(U = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}\)
Step 1: \(U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 10^{-12}}{0.2} = 0.18\) J
Common mistake: 0.9 J (B) divides by \(r^2\), as for the force.
Key point: Like charges have positive potential energy.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Work to turn a coil 60° away from stable equilibrium
questions.question: A coil of 100 turns and area 10 cm² carries 1 A in a uniform field of 0.5 T. The work needed to turn it from stable equilibrium through \(60^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.025 J
Given: \(m = NIA = 100 \times 1 \times 10^{-3} = 0.1\) A m², \(B = 0.5\) T
Formula: \(W = mB(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)\)
Step 1: \(W = 0.1 \times 0.5 \times (1 - \cos 60^\circ)\)
Step 2: \(W = 0.05 \times 0.5 = 0.025\) J
Common mistake: 0.043 J (B) uses \(mB\sin 60^\circ\), the torque in the final position, not the work.
Key point: Work equals the change in \(-mB\cos\theta\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Net field between two wires carrying 10 A and 20 A the same way
questions.question: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 10 A and 20 A in the same direction. The magnetic field at a point between them, 4 cm from the 10 A wire, is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1.67 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Given: \(r_1 = 0.04\) m, \(r_2 = 0.06\) m
Formula: \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\); between same-direction currents the fields point opposite ways
Step 1: \(B_1 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{0.04} = 5 \times 10^{-5}\) T; \(B_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20}{0.06} \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Step 2: \(B = 6.67 \times 10^{-5} - 5 \times 10^{-5} \approx 1.67 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Common mistake: \(1.17 \times 10^{-4}\) T (A) adds the fields, which applies to opposite currents.
Key point: Use the right-hand rule for each wire before combining.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Charge-to-mass ratio of an ion from its accelerating voltage and radius
questions.question: An ion accelerated from rest through 1000 V moves in a circle of radius 10 cm in a perpendicular field of 0.1 T. Its charge-to-mass ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(2 \times 10^{7}\) C kg⁻¹
Given: \(V = 1000\) V, \(r = 0.1\) m, \(B = 0.1\) T
Formula: \(qV = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) and \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\) give \(\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{2V}{B^2r^2}\)
Step 1: \(B^2r^2 = 0.01 \times 0.01 = 10^{-4}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{2000}{10^{-4}} = 2 \times 10^7\) C kg⁻¹
Common mistake: \(1 \times 10^{7}\) (B) drops the 2. \(1.76 \times 10^{11}\) (D) is the electron's value.
Key point: Eliminate \(v\) between the energy and radius equations.

questions.sub_topic: Wavelength of a photon that ionises hydrogen with energy to spare
questions.question: A photon ionises a hydrogen atom in its ground state, and the freed electron has 1.4 eV of kinetic energy. The photon's wavelength is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 82.7 nm
Given: ionisation energy 13.6 eV, \(K = 1.4\) eV
Formula: \(E = 13.6 + K\), \(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E}\)
Step 1: \(E = 15\) eV
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{15} \approx 82.7\) nm
Common mistake: 91.2 nm (B) is the bare ionisation limit. 101 nm (C) subtracts the 1.4 eV.
Key point: Energy beyond 13.6 eV goes into the electron's motion.

questions.sub_topic: Current in a series RC circuit with equal R and X_C
questions.question: A \(100\ \Omega\) resistor and a capacitor of \(\dfrac{100}{\pi}\ \mu\text{F}\) are in series on a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The rms current is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.56 A
Given: \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times \frac{10^{-4}}{\pi}} = 100\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2}\), \(I = \dfrac{V}{Z}\)
Step 1: \(Z = 100\sqrt{2} \approx 141\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{220}{141} \approx 1.56\) A
Common mistake: 1.1 A (B) adds \(R\) and \(X_C\) directly. 2.2 A (C) ignores the capacitor.
Key point: Resistance and reactance combine at right angles.

questions.sub_topic: Voltage that holds a charged oil drop still between plates
questions.question: An oil drop of mass \(3.2 \times 10^{-15}\) kg carries 4 extra electrons. It is held stationary between horizontal plates 5 mm apart. The voltage across the plates is (\(g = 9.8\) m s⁻²):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 245 V
Given: \(q = 4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 6.4 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(d = 5 \times 10^{-3}\) m
Formula: \(qE = mg\), \(V = Ed\)
Step 1: \(E = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 9.8}{6.4 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.9 \times 10^4\) V m⁻¹
Step 2: \(V = 4.9 \times 10^4 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 245\) V
Common mistake: 980 V (C) uses a single electron's charge. \(4.9 \times 10^{4}\) (D) is the field in V m⁻¹, not the voltage.
Key point: The electric force on the drop balances its weight.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: The field of a long solenoid — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The field inside a long ideal solenoid is nearly uniform.
(B) Just outside a long solenoid, near its middle, the field is nearly zero.
(C) At the same turns per unit length and current, a solenoid of larger radius has a stronger field inside.
(D) The field at either end of a long solenoid is about half the field at its middle.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: \(B = \mu_0nI\) contains no radius, so the field does not depend on the solenoid's radius.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) follow from Ampere's law for a long solenoid. (D) at an end there is solenoid on one side only. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The inside field depends only on turns per metre and current.

questions.sub_topic: How resistivity depends on material and temperature — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The resistivity of a metal increases with temperature.
(B) The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases with temperature.
(C) Manganin is used for standard resistors because its resistivity hardly changes with temperature.
(D) The resistivity of a wire doubles when its length is doubled.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) faster ion vibrations shorten the relaxation time. (B) more carriers are freed as temperature rises. (C) its small temperature coefficient keeps its value steady.
Why not the others: (D) is false: resistivity depends only on the material and temperature; doubling the length doubles the resistance, not the resistivity. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Resistance depends on shape; resistivity does not.

questions.sub_topic: Resultant field at the corner of two charges placed at right angles
questions.question: Charges of \(+1\ \mu\text{C}\) each are placed at (3 cm, 0) and (0, 4 cm). The magnitude of the electric field at the origin is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1.15 \times 10^{7}\) N C⁻¹
Given: \(r_1 = 0.03\) m, \(r_2 = 0.04\) m; the two fields are at right angles
Formula: \(E = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}\); \(E_{net} = \sqrt{E_1^2 + E_2^2}\)
Step 1: \(E_1 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^3}{9 \times 10^{-4}} = 1 \times 10^7\); \(E_2 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^3}{1.6 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 5.6 \times 10^6\) N C⁻¹
Step 2: \(E_{net} = \sqrt{10^{14} + 3.2 \times 10^{13}} \approx 1.15 \times 10^7\) N C⁻¹
Common mistake: \(1.56 \times 10^{7}\) (B) adds the magnitudes as if the fields were parallel.
Key point: Fields add as vectors.

questions.sub_topic: Electric force between two protons compared with their gravitational pull
questions.question: The ratio of the electric repulsion to the gravitational attraction between two protons is about (\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m² kg⁻², \(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1.24 \times 10^{36}\)
Given: \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg
Formula: \(\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{ke^2}{Gm_p^2}\) (the distance cancels)
Step 1: \(ke^2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38} = 2.3 \times 10^{-28}\); \(Gm_p^2 = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 2.79 \times 10^{-54} = 1.86 \times 10^{-64}\)
Step 2: Ratio \(\approx 1.24 \times 10^{36}\)
Common mistake: \(2.3 \times 10^{39}\) (B) is the ratio for an electron and a proton; \(4.2 \times 10^{42}\) (C) is for two electrons.
Key point: Gravity is negligible between charged particles.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Angle at which a helix's pitch equals its circumference
questions.question: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity at angle \(\theta\) to the field and moves on a helix. The pitch of the helix equals the circumference of its circular cross-section when \(\theta\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(45^\circ\)
Given: \(T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\), \(r = \dfrac{mv\sin\theta}{qB}\)
Formula: pitch \(= v\cos\theta \times T\); circumference \(= 2\pi r\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2\pi mv\cos\theta}{qB} = \dfrac{2\pi mv\sin\theta}{qB}\), so \(\tan\theta = 1\)
Step 2: \(\theta = 45^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(90^\circ\) (D) gives a flat circle with zero pitch.
Key point: The parallel component sets the pitch; the perpendicular component sets the radius.

questions.sub_topic: Temperature coefficient from resistances at 20 °C and 70 °C
questions.question: A wire's resistance is \(10.0\ \Omega\) at \(20^\circ\)C and \(12.0\ \Omega\) at \(70^\circ\)C. Taking \(R = R_0(1 + \alpha t)\), with \(R_0\) its value at \(0^\circ\)C, the temperature coefficient \(\alpha\) is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(4.35 \times 10^{-3}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)
Given: \(10 = R_0(1 + 20\alpha)\), \(12 = R_0(1 + 70\alpha)\)
Formula: divide to remove \(R_0\)
Step 1: \(1.2(1 + 20\alpha) = 1 + 70\alpha\), so \(0.2 = 46\alpha\)
Step 2: \(\alpha \approx 4.35 \times 10^{-3}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)
Common mistake: \(4.0 \times 10^{-3}\) (B) takes the 20 °C value as \(R_0\).
Key point: \(\alpha\) is defined relative to the resistance at \(0^\circ\)C.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: de Broglie wavelength of the fastest photoelectrons from 200 nm light
questions.question: Light of wavelength 200 nm falls on a metal of work function 4.7 eV. The de Broglie wavelength of the fastest photoelectrons is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.0 nm
Given: \(E = \dfrac{1240}{200} = 6.2\) eV, \(\phi_0 = 4.7\) eV
Formula: \(K_{max} = E - \phi_0\); for an electron \(\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{K}}\) nm, with \(K\) in eV
Step 1: \(K_{max} = 1.5\) eV
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{1.5}} \approx 1.0\) nm
Common mistake: 0.49 nm (C) uses the photon's 6.2 eV as the electron's energy. 200 nm (D) is the light's wavelength.
Key point: Find the electron's energy first, then its wavelength.

questions.sub_topic: Four hydrogen photon energies in increasing order
questions.question:
Arrange these hydrogen emissions in increasing order of photon energy:
(A) the first Balmer line (\(3 \to 2\))
(B) the first Lyman line (\(2 \to 1\))
(C) the first Paschen line (\(4 \to 3\))
(D) the Lyman series limit (\(\infty \to 1\))
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (A), (B), (D)
Step 1: (C) \(1.51 - 0.85 = 0.66\) eV; (A) \(3.40 - 1.51 = 1.89\) eV
Step 2: (B) \(13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2\) eV; (D) 13.6 eV
Step 3: Increasing: (C), (A), (B), (D)
Common mistake: (B) is in decreasing order of energy.
Key point: Jumps to lower final levels release more energy.

questions.sub_topic: Speed gained by a charge repelled to a great distance
questions.question: A particle of mass 2 g carrying \(+2\ \mu\text{C}\) is released from rest 10 cm from a fixed charge of \(+10\ \mu\text{C}\). Ignoring gravity, its speed when it is very far away is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 42.4 m s⁻¹
Given: \(q = 2 \times 10^{-6}\) C, \(Q = 10^{-5}\) C, \(r = 0.1\) m, \(m = 2 \times 10^{-3}\) kg
Formula: \(\dfrac{kqQ}{r} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) (all the potential energy becomes kinetic)
Step 1: \(U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{-5}}{0.1} = 1.8\) J
Step 2: \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.8}{2 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{1800} \approx 42.4\) m s⁻¹
Common mistake: 30 m s⁻¹ (A) drops the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in the kinetic energy.
Key point: Far away the potential energy is zero, so all of it has become kinetic energy.

questions.sub_topic: Parallel trio, mixed trio, pair and balanced bridge ranked by R
questions.question:
Arrange these networks of \(6\ \Omega\) resistors in increasing order of equivalent resistance:
(A) three in parallel
(B) one in series with two that are in parallel
(C) two in parallel
(D) five forming a balanced Wheatstone bridge, measured across the bridge
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (C), (D), (B)
Step 1: (A) \(\dfrac{6}{3} = 2\ \Omega\); (C) \(\dfrac{6}{2} = 3\ \Omega\)
Step 2: (B) \(6 + 3 = 9\ \Omega\); (D) the middle arm carries no current, leaving two \(12\ \Omega\) paths in parallel: \(6\ \Omega\)
Step 3: Increasing: (A), (C), (D), (B)
Common mistake: (A) ranks the bridge as the largest because it has the most resistors.
Key point: Remove the middle arm of a balanced bridge before combining.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Wavelength that triples the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons
questions.question: Light of 3 eV photons ejects photoelectrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 1 eV from a metal. The wavelength of light that would give a maximum kinetic energy of 3 eV is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 248 nm
Given: \(\phi_0 = 3 - 1 = 2\) eV
Formula: \(E = K_{max} + \phi_0\), \(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E}\)
Step 1: \(E = 3 + 2 = 5\) eV
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{5} = 248\) nm
Common mistake: 138 nm (A) triples the photon energy to 9 eV; the work function is not tripled.
Key point: \(K_{max}\) grows linearly with photon energy but is not proportional to it.

questions.sub_topic: Self-inductance of a solenoid rewound with twice the turns
questions.question: A long solenoid is rewound with twice as many turns over the same length and cross-section. Its self-inductance becomes:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) four times as large
Given: \(l\) and \(A\) unchanged, \(N \to 2N\)
Formula: \(L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}\)
Step 1: \(L \propto N^2\)
Step 2: \(L' = 4L\)
Common mistake: Twice (A) forgets that more turns both make more flux and link more of it.
Key point: Self-inductance grows as the square of the turns.

questions.sub_topic: Least deviation produced by an equilateral prism with n equal to root 2
questions.question: An equilateral glass prism is made of material with \(n = \sqrt{2}\). What is the smallest deviation it can give a ray passing through it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(30^\circ\)
Given: \(A = 60^\circ\), \(n = \sqrt{2}\)
Formula: \(n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}\)
Step 1: \(\sin\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2} = \sqrt{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.707\), so \(\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2} = 45^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\delta_m = 30^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(45^\circ\) (B) stops at the half-angle.
Key point: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism.

questions.sub_topic: Average power drawn by a pure inductor on the mains
questions.question: A pure inductor of 0.1 H is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The average power it draws is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) zero
Given: pure inductor, so \(\phi = 90^\circ\)
Formula: \(P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi\)
Step 1: \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), so \(P = 0\)
Common mistake: 1540 W (A) multiplies \(V_{rms}\) by \(I_{rms} \approx 7\) A, ignoring the phase.
Key point: An ideal inductor stores and returns energy each cycle.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Features of photoelectric graphs
questions.question:
Match each feature in List-I with what it gives in List-II.

List-I
(A) Slope of the stopping potential against frequency graph
(B) Intercept of that graph on the frequency axis
(C) Intercept of that line, extended, on the stopping-potential axis
(D) Photocurrent against intensity at a fixed frequency above threshold

List-II
(I) a straight line through the origin
(II) \(-\dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)
(III) \(\dfrac{h}{e}\)
(IV) the threshold frequency \(\nu_0\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Step 1: \(V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\) has slope \(\dfrac{h}{e}\) (III)
Step 2: \(V_0 = 0\) at \(\nu = \nu_0\) (IV)
Step 3: At \(\nu = 0\) the line meets the axis at \(-\dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\) (II)
Step 4: Photocurrent is proportional to intensity (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (C), the two intercepts.
Key point: The slope is the same for every metal; the intercepts depend on the metal.

questions.sub_topic: Secondary values of an ideal 1 : 5 transformer
questions.question:
An ideal transformer has 100 primary turns and 500 secondary turns. The primary takes 10 A at 220 V. Match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I
(A) Secondary voltage
(B) Secondary current
(C) Power delivered to the load
(D) Ratio \(\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}\)

List-II
(I) 5
(II) 2200 W
(III) 2 A
(IV) 1100 V
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 5\) (I)
Step 2: \(V_s = 5 \times 220 = 1100\) V (IV)
Step 3: \(I_s = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\) A (III)
Step 4: \(P = 220 \times 10 = 2200\) W, the same on both sides (II)
Common mistake: Stepping the current up along with the voltage; that would create energy.
Key point: A step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current.

questions.sub_topic: Inductance of a coil from its d.c. and a.c. currents
questions.question: A coil draws 2 A from a 12 V d.c. supply and 1.2 A (rms) from a 12 V (rms), 50 Hz a.c. supply. Its self-inductance is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 25.5 mH
Given: d.c. gives \(R = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6\ \Omega\); a.c. gives \(Z = \dfrac{12}{1.2} = 10\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(X_L = \sqrt{Z^2 - R^2}\), \(L = \dfrac{X_L}{2\pi\nu}\)
Step 1: \(X_L = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(L = \dfrac{8}{314} \approx 25.5\) mH
Common mistake: 31.8 mH (A) uses \(Z\) as the reactance. 0.16 H (D) divides by 50 instead of \(2\pi \times 50\).
Key point: d.c. reveals the resistance; a.c. reveals the impedance.

questions.sub_topic: What stays fixed when a 600 nm beam enters a 1.5-index slab
questions.question: A beam whose wavelength in air is 600 nm passes into a slab of index 1.5. How many oscillations per second does it make inside the slab?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz
Given: \(\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-7}\) m in air
Formula: \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\), unchanged on refraction
Step 1: \(\nu = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{6 \times 10^{-7}} = 5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz
Common mistake: \(7.5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz (B) multiplies by \(n\); only the speed and wavelength change.
Key point: Frequency is fixed by the source.

questions.sub_topic: Object distance for an erect image three times the size in a convex lens
questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 15 cm forms an erect image three times the size of the object. The object is at:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10 cm
Given: erect image, so \(m = +3\) and \(v = 3u\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{3u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{2}{3u} = \dfrac{1}{15}\)
Step 2: \(u = -10\) cm, i.e. 10 cm from the lens
Common mistake: 20 cm (A) is the answer for an inverted, real image three times the size.
Key point: An erect image from a convex lens means the object is inside \(f\).

questions.sub_topic: Ionisation energy of ground-state hydrogen in joules
questions.question: The energy needed to ionise a hydrogen atom from its ground state, in joules, is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2.18 \times 10^{-18}\) J
Given: ionisation energy 13.6 eV
Formula: 1 eV \(= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J
Step 1: \(13.6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \approx 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\) J
Common mistake: \(8.5 \times 10^{-20}\) J (B) divides by the conversion factor.
Key point: Multiply eV by \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) to get joules.

questions.sub_topic: Maxwell's results for electromagnetic waves
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II.

List-I
(A) Speed of EM waves in vacuum
(B) Speed of EM waves in a medium
(C) Direction of propagation
(D) Displacement current

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}\)
(II) \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\)
(III) \(\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\)
(IV) along \(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Step 1: In vacuum \(c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\) (II)
Step 2: In a medium \(v = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}\) (I)
Step 3: The wave travels along \(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\) (IV)
Step 4: \(i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\) (III)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); the subscript 0 marks the vacuum values.
Key point: Maxwell's equations predict the speed of light from \(\mu_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\).

questions.sub_topic: Changes when a wire is stretched to twice its length
questions.question:
A wire is stretched uniformly to twice its length (its volume stays the same) and is then connected to the same voltage. Match each quantity in List-I with the factor by which it changes in List-II.

List-I
(A) Resistance
(B) Resistivity
(C) Cross-sectional area
(D) Current

List-II
(I) unchanged
(II) one quarter
(III) four times
(IV) half
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Fixed volume: \(A\) halves when \(l\) doubles (IV)
Step 2: \(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}\) becomes \(2 \times 2 = 4\) times (III)
Step 3: Resistivity is a property of the material (I)
Step 4: \(I = \dfrac{V}{R}\) falls to one quarter (II)
Common mistake: Taking the resistance as doubled, forgetting that the area also halves.
Key point: Stretching changes length and area together.

questions.sub_topic: Charge, voltages and energy of a 3 μF–6 μF series pair on 90 V
questions.question:
Capacitors of \(3\ \mu\text{F}\) and \(6\ \mu\text{F}\) are connected in series across a 90 V supply. Match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I
(A) Charge on the \(3\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor
(B) Voltage across the \(3\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor
(C) Voltage across the \(6\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor
(D) Total energy stored

List-II
(I) 30 V
(II) \(180\ \mu\text{C}\)
(III) 8.1 mJ
(IV) 60 V
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(C_{eq} = \dfrac{3 \times 6}{9} = 2\ \mu\text{F}\); each capacitor carries \(Q = 2 \times 90 = 180\ \mu\text{C}\) (II)
Step 2: \(V_3 = \dfrac{180}{3} = 60\) V (IV)
Step 3: \(V_6 = \dfrac{180}{6} = 30\) V (I)
Step 4: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 90^2 = 8.1\) mJ (III)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (C); in series the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage.
Key point: Series capacitors share the same charge, not the same voltage.

questions.sub_topic: Apparent position of a fish near the wall of a spherical bowl
questions.question: A spherical fish bowl of radius 15 cm is filled with water (\(n = \dfrac{4}{3}\)). A fish is 5 cm from the near wall, on the diameter through the observer. Ignoring the thin glass, the fish appears to be:
options: D) about 4.1 cm inside the wall
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) about 4.1 cm inside the wall
Given: light goes water → air; \(n_1 = \dfrac{4}{3}\), \(n_2 = 1\), \(u = -5\) cm; the centre is on the water side, so \(R = -15\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{4}{15} = \dfrac{-1/3}{-15} = \dfrac{1}{45}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1 - 12}{45}\), so \(v \approx -4.1\) cm (virtual, inside the bowl)
Common mistake: 3.75 cm (A) treats the wall as flat. 3.5 cm (C) takes \(R\) as \(+15\) cm.
Key point: Fix the sign of \(R\) from where the centre lies relative to the incoming light.

questions.sub_topic: Forward and reverse bias of a junction — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Forward bias lowers the potential barrier of a p–n junction.
(B) Reverse bias widens the depletion region.
(C) The small reverse current is carried by minority carriers.
(D) Under forward bias the current is carried mainly by minority carriers.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: under forward bias, majority carriers diffuse across the lowered barrier and carry the current.
Why not the others: (A) the applied voltage opposes the barrier. (B) it pulls carriers away from the junction. (C) the barrier blocks majority carriers. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Forward current is majority-carrier diffusion; reverse current is minority-carrier drift.

questions.sub_topic: Distance of the second minimum from the centre of a single-slit pattern
questions.question: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls on a slit 0.1 mm wide. On a screen 2 m away, the second minimum lies from the centre of the pattern at:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2 cm
Given: \(a = 10^{-4}\) m, \(\lambda = 5 \times 10^{-7}\) m, \(D = 2\) m
Formula: minima at \(a\sin\theta = n\lambda\), so \(y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{a}\)
Step 1: \(y_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 5 \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{10^{-4}}\)
Step 2: \(y_2 = 0.02\) m \(= 2\) cm
Common mistake: 4 cm (C) is the gap between the second minima on either side.
Key point: Single-slit minima come at whole numbers of wavelengths.

questions.sub_topic: Momentum, medium and frequency of EM waves — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) EM waves carry momentum and can exert pressure on a surface.
(B) EM waves need no material medium to travel.
(C) The frequency of light does not change when it passes from air into glass.
(D) In vacuum, X-rays travel faster than radio waves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) absorbed or reflected waves transfer momentum. (B) the fields sustain each other. (C) frequency is set by the source.
Why not the others: (D) is false: every EM wave travels at \(c\) in vacuum. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: All EM waves share one speed in vacuum.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Moment of each half of a bar magnet cut across its length
questions.question: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 4 A m² is cut into two equal halves perpendicular to its length. The magnetic moment of each half is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 A m²
Given: \(m = q_m \times 2l = 4\) A m²
Formula: each half keeps the pole strength but has half the length
Step 1: \(m' = q_m \times l = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\) A m²
Common mistake: 4 A m² (A) assumes each piece keeps the whole moment.
Key point: Cutting never isolates a single pole; each piece is a new dipole.

questions.sub_topic: Voltage across the capacitor in a resonant series circuit
questions.question: A series LCR circuit on a 230 V supply is at resonance, and the voltage across the inductor is 400 V. The voltage across the capacitor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 400 V
Given: at resonance \(X_L = X_C\)
Formula: \(V_L = IX_L\), \(V_C = IX_C\)
Step 1: Same current and equal reactances, so \(V_C = V_L = 400\) V
Step 2: The two cancel, leaving all 230 V across \(R\)
Common mistake: 170 V (A) subtracts the supply voltage from \(V_L\).
Key point: At resonance \(V_L\) and \(V_C\) can each exceed the supply.

questions.sub_topic: Nuclear size and density — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The radius of a nucleus is proportional to \(A^{1/3}\).
(B) Nuclear density is roughly the same for all nuclei.
(C) Nuclear density is about \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\) kg m⁻³.
(D) Doubling the mass number doubles the nuclear radius.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(R = R_0A^{1/3}\). (B) volume grows in step with mass. (C) \(\dfrac{m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\) kg m⁻³.
Why not the others: (D) is false: doubling \(A\) raises \(R\) by \(2^{1/3} \approx 1.26\). Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Nucleons pack like drops of an incompressible liquid.

questions.sub_topic: Least refractive index for total reflection in a right-angled prism
questions.question: Light enters one short face of a right-angled isosceles glass prism at normal incidence and meets the hypotenuse face. The least refractive index for which it is totally reflected there is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.414
Given: the ray meets the hypotenuse at \(45^\circ\)
Formula: total reflection needs \(i \ge C\), with \(\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n}\)
Step 1: \(\sin 45^\circ \ge \dfrac{1}{n}\)
Step 2: \(n \ge \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\)
Common mistake: 1.5 (C) is a typical value for glass, not the minimum.
Key point: Such prisms turn light through \(90^\circ\) in binoculars.

questions.sub_topic: Fringe width after changing the wavelength, slit gap and screen distance
questions.question: In a double-slit experiment the fringe width is 0.6 mm with light of 600 nm. The light is changed to 400 nm, the slit separation is halved and the screen distance is doubled. The new fringe width is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.6 mm
Given: \(\lambda: \times \dfrac{2}{3}\), \(d: \times \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(D: \times 2\)
Formula: \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)
Step 1: Factor \(= \dfrac{2}{3} \times 2 \times 2 = \dfrac{8}{3}\)
Step 2: \(\beta' = 0.6 \times \dfrac{8}{3} = 1.6\) mm
Common mistake: 2.4 mm (A) ignores the change of wavelength. 3.6 mm (B) inverts the wavelength ratio.
Key point: Apply each factor according to where it sits in \(\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Field at the centre of a quarter-circle arc of current
questions.question: A wire carrying 5 A is bent into a quarter circle of radius 10 cm, with its straight leads running radially towards the centre. The magnetic field at the centre is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(7.85 \times 10^{-6}\) T
Given: \(I = 5\) A, \(R = 0.1\) m, the arc is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of a circle
Formula: \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R} \times \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}\); the radial leads add nothing
Step 1: Full loop: \(\dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5}{0.2} \approx 3.14 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Step 2: Quarter: \(\approx 7.85 \times 10^{-6}\) T
Common mistake: \(1.57 \times 10^{-5}\) T (B) treats the arc as a semicircle. \(1 \times 10^{-5}\) T (C) uses the formula for a long straight wire.
Key point: Each element of an arc adds the same field at its centre.

questions.sub_topic: Supply voltage for 10 mA through a silicon diode and 200 Ω
questions.question: A silicon diode (0.7 V drop) is forward biased in series with a \(200\ \Omega\) resistor. For a current of 10 mA the supply voltage must be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2.7 V
Given: \(I = 0.01\) A, \(R = 200\ \Omega\), diode drop 0.7 V
Formula: \(V = IR + V_D\)
Step 1: \(IR = 2.0\) V
Step 2: \(V = 2.0 + 0.7 = 2.7\) V
Common mistake: 2.0 V (A) leaves out the diode's drop.
Key point: The supply must cover the diode drop as well as the resistor.

questions.sub_topic: Heat produced while a battery charges a capacitor
questions.question: A \(5\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is charged from zero by a 100 V battery through a resistor. The heat produced in the resistor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.025 J
Given: \(C = 5 \times 10^{-6}\) F, \(V = 100\) V
Formula: battery work \(= QV\); stored energy \(= \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\)
Step 1: \(Q = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) C; battery work \(= 0.05\) J; stored \(= 0.025\) J
Step 2: Heat \(= 0.05 - 0.025 = 0.025\) J, whatever the resistance
Common mistake: 0.05 J (A) is the battery's total work, half of which is stored.
Key point: Charging through a resistor always wastes half of the battery's work.
